phrases.meaning: Do you have any more of these?
phrases.usageNote: Use when you find something you like but want to check for better options in the back room or stockroom.
Direct follow-up if you are not happy with the condition of the only piece on display.

phrases.japanese: もっといい状態のものはありますか？
phrases.romaji: Motto ii jōtai no mono wa arimasu ka?
phrases.meaning: Do you have this in better condition?
phrases.usageNote: Signals you are a serious buyer willing to pay more for quality. Often prompts staff to check the back.

phrases.japanese: 時計はどこにありますか？
phrases.romaji: Tokei wa doko ni arimasu ka?
phrases.usageNote: Swap 時計 (tokei) for カメラ (kamera), 服 (fuku), or レコード (rekōdo) depending on what you are looking for.
Open-ended. Staff will usually give an honest answer — shops grade items internally and stake their reputation on it.
Stronger than just 動きますか — the word ちゃんと (properly) signals you care about function, not just that it powers on.
Appropriate for luxury items, branded goods, or anything where counterfeits are common. Staff will not be offended.

phrases.japanese: 傷や欠陥はありますか？
phrases.romaji: Kizu ya kekkan wa arimasu ka?
phrases.meaning: Are there any defects or damage?
phrases.usageNote: More thorough than 傷はどこですか — covers both cosmetic and functional issues. Use before buying anything expensive.

phrases.japanese: もう少し安くなりますか？
phrases.meaning: Can you make it a little cheaper?
phrases.usageNote: Polite opener. Use with a smile after a pause. Works about 40% of the time in recycle shops.

phrases.japanese: まとめて買うので、少し負けてもらえますか？
phrases.romaji: Matomete kau node, sukoshi makete moraemasu ka?
phrases.meaning: I'm buying several things — can you give me a small discount?
phrases.usageNote: Most effective phrase when buying 2+ items. Show them the pile before asking.
Essential for unpriced items. Point clearly at what you're asking about.
For electronics, cameras, watches. Simple and universally understood.
Most shops accommodate this request. For cameras, staff may have a battery available.
Forces transparency about flaws. Also signals you're an experienced buyer — often leads to better treatment.
Use after selecting multiple items. Often triggers a spontaneous discount without needing to ask.

phrases.japanese: この３つをまとめてどうですか？
phrases.romaji: Kono mittsu wo matomete dō desu ka?
phrases.meaning: How about these three as a bundle?
phrases.usageNote: Specific and polite. Swap the number: futatsu (2), mittsu (3), yottsu (4), itsutsu (5).

phrases.japanese: 値段がついていないのですが…
phrases.romaji: Nedan ga tsuite inai no desu ga...
phrases.meaning: This doesn't have a price tag...
phrases.usageNote: The trailing ellipsis is intentional. Pause after saying it — let them fill the silence with a price.

phrases.japanese: これはいくらで売ってもらえますか？
phrases.romaji: Kore wa ikura de utte moraemasu ka?
phrases.meaning: How much would you sell this for?
phrases.usageNote: More direct version. Use for display cases or items behind glass.
The most useful phrase of all. Clear and polite — staff will immediately start processing the sale.
Most Hard Off and 2nd Street chains accept cards. Smaller independent shops are often cash only.
Japan introduced a plastic bag charge in 2020. Staff may not offer one automatically — ask if you need it.

phrases.japanese: 領収書をいただけますか？
phrases.usageNote: Essential for customs declarations. Keep all receipts when buying items you plan to resell.

phrases.japanese: 見ているだけです、ありがとう。
phrases.usageNote: Use when approached by staff and you are not ready to buy. Polite and gives you space to browse.
Use when walking away without offense. Often prompts a last-minute counteroffer from the seller.

phrases.japanese: ありがとうございました
phrases.usageNote: Always end with this regardless of outcome. Keeps the relationship warm for next time.
Regular visitors get better treatment. Staff remember faces and become more flexible over multiple visits.
